title: How logins work
summary: What really happens when someone logs in: password hashing, "Sign in with Google" and magic links, and the mistakes that leak accounts.
youWillLearn: Why an app should never store a password, and what it stores instead
What salt and a slow hash add, and why bcrypt or Argon2 beat a plain hash
How Sign in with Google works without Notely ever seeing the Google password
How magic links work, and what to check on the login form itself

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast. Notely's is Postgres, run by Supabase.
glossary.authentication: Proving who you are, for example by typing the right password. Deciding what you may do comes later.
glossary.hash: A fixed-length fingerprint computed from some input. The same input always gives the same hash, and you cannot turn the hash back into the input.
glossary.salt: A random value stored next to each user's hash and mixed into it, so two people with the same password get different hashes.
glossary.bcrypt: A password hashing function that is slow on purpose, with an adjustable cost. Argon2 and scrypt are newer siblings built for the same job.
glossary.OAuth: A standard that lets one app act on, or log you in with, your account at another service, without ever getting that service's password.
glossary.OpenID Connect: The login layer on top of OAuth. It adds a signed statement of who the user is, which is what "Sign in with Google" uses.
glossary.identity provider: The service that checks the password and vouches for the user: Google, Apple, GitHub, or your own auth server.
glossary.redirect URL: The address an identity provider sends the user back to after login. It must be on a list you registered in advance.
glossary.magic link: A login link sent by email. It holds a long random token that works once and expires after a short time.
glossary.credential stuffing: Bots trying email and password pairs leaked from other sites, hoping people reused them on yours.
glossary.MFA: Multi-factor authentication: a second proof after the password, like a code from an authenticator app.

steps.title: Maya signs up for Notely
body: Notely is the notes app we build in this course. Maya signs up: she types her email and a password into her browser on her laptop.
The browser sends them to the app server (the computer running Notely's code). It saves them in the database, which keeps Notely's data. For now, the password is saved exactly as typed.

callout.text: New to Notely? The 4-minute Meet Notely lesson at the start of the Data module shows the whole app, part by part.

scene.caption: Maya's email and password travel to the app server, which saves them in the database.

steps.title: One leaked copy exposes everyone
body: Notely now has 10,000 users. One day a copy of the database ends up in the wrong hands: a stolen backup, a bad query, a hacked laptop.
The attacker can read every password. People reuse passwords, so Maya's email account is now at risk too.

callout.text: A leak is not a rare disaster you can plan around. Assume your database will be copied one day, and make sure the copy is useless.

changes: + Stolen Copy: the database, copied by an attacker
~ Passwords known 0 → 10,000
~ Browser steps back

scene.caption: One stolen copy, and every password in it is readable.

steps.title: Store a fingerprint, not the password
body: Notely never needs to read Maya's password again. It only needs to check that she typed the same one. So at sign-up it stores a hash: a one-way fingerprint of the password.
At login it hashes what she typed and compares. Same fingerprint: she is in. That check is authentication.

callout.text: A fingerprint can prove a person was here, but you cannot rebuild the person from it. A password hash works the same way.

changes: ~ Database: password → hash
~ Passwords known 10,000 → 4,000
~ Stolen Copy: only weak passwords can be matched

scene.caption: The database holds fingerprints. Most of the stolen copy is now useless.

steps.title: Salt and slowness: the real recipe
body: Why 4,000? Attackers keep huge lists of common passwords already hashed, and a plain hash of password123 is the same for everyone. So each user gets a random salt mixed in.
And the hash is slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2. One login barely notices. A billion guesses become very expensive.

callout.text: Never write your own hashing. Let the auth service do it, or use a well-known library for bcrypt or Argon2.

code.caption: $2a$ means bcrypt, 10 is the cost. Salt and hash live in one string. Same password, different strings.

changes: ~ Database: plain hash → salted bcrypt
~ Passwords known 4,000 → 20: the weakest, one slow guess at a time

scene.caption: Salted, slow hashes: every guess costs the attacker real time.

steps.title: Sign in with Google: no password at all
body: Better still: do not hold passwords. With Sign in with Google, Google checks Maya's password and tells Notely who she is. Google is the identity provider.
The standard behind this is OAuth, and its login layer is OpenID Connect. Notely never sees Maya's Google password, so it cannot leak it.

callout.text: A hotel that accepts your passport instead of issuing its own ID card. It trusts that the government already checked who you are.

changes: + Google: checks Maya's password for Notely
− Stolen Copy
~ Database: no password at all for Maya

scene.caption: Maya logs in at Google. Notely's database holds no password for her.

steps.title: The redirect dance, step by step
body: Notely sends Maya's browser to Google. She logs in there. Google sends her back to Notely's redirect URL with a one-time code.
The app server then trades that code with Google for her verified identity. The code works once, expires fast, and is useless without a second proof the server kept back.
changes: + Arrow: Google sends Maya back with a one-time code
+ Arrow: the app server trades the code for her identity
~ Database steps back

scene.caption: Google returns a one-time code. The app server trades it for Maya's identity.

steps.title: Redirect URLs must be on a list
body: Google, and Supabase in front of it, only send codes back to redirect URLs you registered in advance. That stops an attacker from having Maya's code delivered to their own site.
The classic bug: login works on localhost (your own laptop), then fails on the live site, because nobody added its address to the list.

callout.text: Do not "fix" a failing redirect with a wildcard that matches any domain. Add the exact production URL, and keep any preview wildcard tied to your own team's domain.

changes: + Fake Site: an attacker's page asking for Maya's code
~ Google refuses: the fake address is not on the list

scene.caption: Google only hands codes to addresses on the list. The fake site gets nothing.

steps.title: Magic links: the inbox is the key
body: Another password-free option: Maya types her email, and Notely sends her a magic link. It holds a long random code that works once and expires soon. Clicking it logs her in.
The trade-off: whoever can read Maya's inbox can log in as her. That was already true, since every "forgot password" email works the same way.
changes: + Maya's Inbox: her email, where the link arrives
− Google and Fake Site
~ Database back in view

scene.caption: Notely emails a one-time link. Clicking it brings the code back to the app server.

steps.title: The login form leaks too
body: "No account for this email" tells an attacker who uses Notely. Say "Wrong email or password" in both cases.

And bots run credential stuffing: they replay email and password pairs leaked from other sites. Limit login attempts, and offer MFA, a second proof like an app code, so a correct password alone is not enough.

callout.text: You met rate limiting in the system design course. A login form is one of the first places it belongs, counted per account and per IP address.

changes: + Bot: replays passwords leaked from other sites
− Maya's Inbox
~ App Server: login attempts limited

scene.caption: A bot hammers the login form. The attempt limit and MFA stop it.

steps.title: Recap: hand it all to an auth service
body: Notely writes none of this itself. Supabase Auth, the login service that comes with Notely's database, stores salted bcrypt hashes, runs the Google flow, sends magic links and limits attempts.
Notely calls one function per method. Next lesson: how the browser proves, request after request, that Maya is still logged in.

callout.text: Ask: does any of our own tables have a password column? (It should not.) Are the live and preview URLs in Supabase's Redirect URLs? Does /auth/callback call exchangeCodeForSession? Is anything logging login request bodies?

changes: + Supabase Auth: the login service next to the database
− Bot
~ App Server hands every login to Supabase Auth

scene.caption: Three login methods, one auth service. Notely's own tables hold no passwords.

quiz.question: Claude Code drafts a profiles table with a password column and plans to compare it with what the user types. What do you ask for instead?

options.text: Encrypt the column with a key stored in an env var.
options.why: Encryption can be reversed by anyone who gets the key, and the server needs that key at hand. Passwords should never be recoverable at all.

options.text: Hash it with SHA-256 before saving.
options.why: Better than plain text, but SHA-256 is fast and unsalted here. Attackers can test billions of guesses per second against it.

options.text: Drop the column and use Supabase Auth, which stores salted bcrypt hashes.
options.why: A proven auth service salts and slow-hashes passwords for you, and keeps them out of your own tables.

quiz.question: "Sign in with Google" works on localhost but fails on the live site with a redirect error. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The live site's URL is missing from the allowed redirect URLs.
options.why: Google and Supabase only send users back to addresses registered in advance. Add the exact production URL to both lists.

options.text: Google blocks logins from sites hosted on Vercel.
options.why: Google does not care where a site is hosted. It only checks that the redirect URL is on your registered list.

options.text: Maya's Google password is not stored on the live site yet.
options.why: Notely never stores Google passwords. Google checks the password itself.

quiz.question: A client wants to drop passwords and use only magic links. What changes about the account's security?

options.text: Nothing can go wrong, because there is no password to steal.
options.why: The link itself is now the key. Anyone who reads the inbox, or intercepts the link before it expires, can log in.
You can and should limit how often links are requested per email and per IP, so the form cannot be used to spam inboxes.

options.text: Account safety now depends on the user's email inbox.
options.why: Whoever controls the inbox can log in. This was already true for password resets, so it is often a fair trade.

takeaways: Never store passwords. Store a salted, slow hash (bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2) and compare hashes at login.
Do not write your own auth. Let Supabase Auth or another proven service hash, verify and email for you.
Sign in with Google uses OAuth and OpenID Connect: Google checks the password, your app gets a verified identity.
Register exact redirect URLs for production and previews. Avoid wide wildcards.
Use one vague error for wrong email or password, limit login attempts, and offer MFA.
